title: Roll Models: Bristol-Based Bikepacking Mentorship for WTNB Riders – Hailey Moore
content:
“In an ideal world, Roll Models would be redundant, we wouldn’t need to create these safe spaces,” says founder Athlyn Cathcart as the Bristol-based bikepacking mentorship group approaches its third year providing community and skills-learning to women, trans, and non-binary identifying cyclists.

For many, commuting serves as the gateway drug into the sport of cycling. It is not uncommon for the workingman’s discipline to awaken in new riders a desire for more, an itch to go further. That oft-cited sense of freedom that even the utilitarian practice of pedaling to and fro—between work, school, and home—gives a sweet taste of is enough to draw novices down a lifelong rabbit hole. This was indeed the case for Athlyn Cathcart, who credits her time commuting during her university years as the portal through which she discovered a much wider world of cycling. A world that she is now actively inviting others to join.

Photo credit: Aphra Evans (left), Abbie Merritt (right)

“I discovered the bike as a way to avoid being underground,” Cathcart said on a recent Zoom call, referring to London’s sprawling Tube system. Born in Toronto, Cathcart spent most of her childhood in the Midlands of England before moving to study Sociology and Politics at Goldsmiths, University of London. You can trace the long-tailed ripple effects of her community-focused studies to the off-the-clock work that she does today with Roll Models, a bikepacking and adventure-riding mentorship organization for WTNB riders.

Cathcart founded the Roll Models bikepacking mentorship in 2024, in Bristol where she now lives, after she’d amassed more than a dozen years of riding experience. The seed planted by her time commuting germinated in chasing bigger, more adventurous rides, and becoming a seasoned bikepacker. Still, it took her a long time to warm up to the notion of solo touring. At some point, Cathcart said she realized, “I’ve been doing this for ten years, but I’ve never solo camped.” Maybe, in a proverbial sense, she was still figuring out how to avoid being underground, how to come up for air. How to be seen, or how to see herself in an industry where she is among the underrepresented. The roots were there, but she realized that cultivating a stronger sense of independence, and maybe sticking her neck out a bit, would allow her to truly flourish.

Photo credit: @Twoevstops

This kind of reticence is exactly what Roll Models aims to help its members overcome. On her hesitation about traveling as a solo woman, Cathcart said that this is broadly a “systemic issue, not a cycling issue,” and that “not seeing yourself reflected in [social] media or whatever it is” can inhibit one’s sense of agency, especially in the vulnerable context of bikepacking.

Once she finally rallied her resolve for a solo tour, Cathcart said she was surprised by the paradox she experienced. The fear that had been curbing her own ambitions gave way to an unmatched sense of escape.

“The way I feel when I’m on a solo trip, I get a sense of freedom that I don’t feel in many other aspects of life,” said Cathcart. “Completely care-free, completely at my own pace and rhythm.”

Photo credit: Abbie Merritt (left); @Twoevstops (right)

This is the feeling that Cathcart wants to impart to members of Roll Models. As a Community Interest Company (a business entity specific to the UK for social enterprises with profits reinvested back in for community benefit), Roll Models operates on the calendar’s cycle, opening its application window in late winter to prospective members interested in participating in its two annual community campouts, workshops, group rides, and other meet-ups that take place throughout the remainder of the year. Roll Models offers a sliding pay scale to members to cover the cost of insurance, reservations, food and other expenses associated with its events.

In its first season, in 2025, Roll Models received 70 applicants for its—at the time—1:1 mentorship cohort. Of those, they accepted 34. This year, they shifted the model from a 1:1 mentor-mentee ratio to a breakdown that favors collective encouragement over a more direct teacher-student dynamic. For every three members, there are two mentors. This lessens the burden on mentors and allows more applicants to participate. Of this year’s 100 applicants, Roll Models had room for 55. Cathcart also says that by placing less emphasis on an experience hierarchy, she hopes to show members that “everyone has something to learn, everyone has something to share.”

Photo credit: Abbie Merritt

Experience among members does span a wide range. Some have never bike camped before, and newcomers often ask what bike and kit they need. Cathcart likes to use her own first “bikepacking” bike—a Bianchi singlespeed road bike—as an example that you don’t need to go out and buy new gear; “I just walked the hills,” she says. For members who have more experience, Cathcart says that she often sees parallels between their confidence levels and those of her earlier self, citing how a member might say that even though they have “cycled across Cuba or Mongolia with my male partner, I don’t think I know enough to be a mentor.”

To accommodate such a broad swath of knowledge levels and abilities, Roll Models sorts members into small groups at the beginning of the year to talk about their past experience and future ambitions. During the organization’s two annual campouts, members can self-select into different pace groups to facilitate an experience that feels accessible and enjoyable to all. The first 2026 campout took place in June and included a 50-kilometer ride from Bristol, following flat bike paths and paved roads (with public transit as an alternate option for part of the route). Once at camp, the group set up tents before an evening of on-bike egg-and-spoon races (a Roll Models staple activity) while Cathcart cooked for everyone.

Photo credit: Aphra Evans (left); Cat Giovanetti (right)

In September, the group spent a weekend in South Wales, setting up shop at a basecamp destination and offering different day-ride options for folks to choose from. Post-ride activities included crafts (tie-dyeing and lino-cut stamp-making), sauna sessions, egg-and-spoon races (of course), and group dinners around a fire.

Photo credit: Aphra Evans

As proof of the demand that Roll Models is feeling from its members, this will be the first year the organization doesn’t take an off-season. Although their campouts are paused until next summer—with applications for 2027 opening in February or March—Cathcart says that they have a calendar of workshops on topics such as safety, bike maintenance, and making your own gear planned to keep the group together through the colder months.

Photo credit: Abbie Merritt

When members for the new year’s cohort are chosen, Cathcart says she often gets asked: “Where do I start with bikepacking?” To which she says, “That has so many different answers… there is no right way of doing this.” Instead of giving a prescriptive response, she prefers to meet question with question, challenging new members to foreground their own goals and emboldening them to consider the unceilinged possibilities: “What do you want to get out of this?”
